name: Social Recon 101
description: We found a suspicious user handle '@GhostAdmin99'. Read through the attached text file to find their digital footprint and the first flag.

name: The GitHub Leak
description:
The target deleted their code, but we managed to scrape a leaked commit note! Decode this Base64 string to see what they were hiding:

dGNze2doX2NvbW1pdF9yZWNvdmVyZWR9

name: Forum Secrets
description:
We found a deleted post on an underground hacker forum. The attacker used a ROT47 cipher to hide their text. Crack it:

E4DlzC49:G6507@CF>0A@DEX

name: Shadow Domain
description:
We found a secret DNS record pointing to a hidden server! Read this intercepted DNS entry carefully to spot the flag:

admin-portal.shadow.tcs{shadow_domain_found}.tcs.local IN A 10.0.0.5

name: Inspect Element
description:
A junior developer was feeling lazy and left a comment directly in the website's HTML code. Can you spot what they accidentally exposed?

<!-- TODO: Remove hardcoded token tcs{html_comments_leak} before go-live -->

name: Sneaky SQLi
clue: Look for SQL injection syntax like OR 1=1.
description: Someone bypassed the login page using a SQL injection! Look through the attached web server logs to find the exact payload they used.

name: Server Pivot
clue: Look for local IPs in the URLs.
description: After breaking into the website, the attacker tricked the server into making a request to the internal network (SSRF). Check the web logs again to find the flag they grabbed.

name: Prototype Pollution
description:
The web app handles user settings really poorly. We caught this malicious JSON payload the attacker sent to give themselves admin rights. Grab the flag from it:

{"__proto__":{"admin":true, "flag":"tcs{js_prototype_polluted}"}}

name: Caesar's Salad
description: This text file contains a secret message. It looks like a random mess of letters, but it's just a classic Caesar cipher shifted by 13. Decrypt it!

name: Vigenère Key
description:
This cipher is a bit tougher because it uses a repeating keyword. Crack the Vigenère cipher below and wrap your answer in tcs{} to get the flag.

Ciphertext: hsnirsphlcvvag_elrgcif
Key: SECURE

name: Weak RSA
clue: Find the factors of the small prime numbers.
description: We found an encrypted message and a public RSA key in this file. The problem? The prime numbers they used are way too small! Factor them out to crack the encryption.

name: Hex to ASCII
clue: Use a Hex to Text converter.
description:
We managed to extract this raw Hexadecimal string from the attacker's memory. Convert the Hex characters back into normal ASCII text to read the flag:

7463737b65636473615f6e6f6e63655f7265757365647d

name: Magic Bytes
clue: Use a hex editor like HxD.
description: We found a PNG image file, but it refuses to open! The first few 'magic bytes' of the file header got corrupted. Fix them in a hex editor to see the image.

name: PCAP Carving
clue: Follow the TCP streams in Wireshark.
description: Two computers were talking on the network, and we recorded it in this PCAP file. Open it in Wireshark and figure out what secret file they were sending to each other.

name: Hidden in the Pixels
clue: Look into LSB (Least Significant Bit) steganography.
description: It looks like a normal picture, but we know there's data hiding inside the pixel colors! Analyze the stego image file to extract the hidden message.

name: Memory Dump
description:
We took a snapshot of a compromised computer's RAM. We found this chunk of data inside the Windows password process (LSASS). Find the flag in the dump:

[+] AuthId: 0;314981 Administrator : tcs{mimikatz_mem_dump}

name: Packet Snooping
clue: Look at the raw packet bytes in Wireshark.
description: Something weird is happening on the local network. Open up the provided PCAP file and dig through the raw packet data to find what the attacker injected.

name: BGP Hijack
description:
Our internet traffic is being routed to the wrong place! We pulled this log showing a fake network path. Can you spot the fake Autonomous System (AS)?

ACTION=REDIRECT PATH=AS100->AS200->tcs{as_path_spoofed}

name: Ping Smuggling
clue: Convert the Hex bytes back into text.
description:
The hacker snuck data right past the firewall by hiding it inside ping requests (ICMP). We grabbed the raw Hex bytes of the payload. Translate it to text to get the flag:

74 63 73 7b 66 72 61 67 6d 65 6e 74 65 64 5f 69 63 6d 70 5f 70 61 79 6c 6f 61 64 7d

name: Secret DNS Chat
description:
The malware is talking to the hacker by making fake DNS requests! Check out this command we caught. Decode the Base64 part to find the hidden flag:

nslookup -type=txt dGNze21hbGljaW91c19kbnNfdHh0fQ==.c2.server.local

name: RockYou Basics
description: Someone dumped a database, and we found an MD5 password hash in the text file. It's a super common password, so a simple dictionary attack should break it easily!

name: Adding Symbols
clue: Wrap the cracked password in tcs{}.
description:
The user got smart and added symbols to their password. Crack this SHA256 hash, then put your answer inside the tcs{} format to submit it:

747c3cfc40ec4debd38031e2fbcc902377b25055b80a47d2197171c77f0a7cb2

name: Local Dictionary
clue: The password is based on the capital city of Pretoria.
description:
This user bases their passwords on their hometown. Crack this MD5 hash using some creative local keywords, then submit it in the tcs{} format:

146bf99cfc1a5d62557ff1709abf3dfd

name: NTLM Relay
clue: Check the text file for the password.
description: We captured a Windows NTLMv2 hash while the attacker was moving across the network. Open the text file and find the admin password they were using.

name: Basic Strings
description: We found a suspicious program file. The developer made a huge mistake and typed the secret password right into the code! Extract the readable text to find the flag.

name: Reading Assembly
clue: Look at the FLAG= section in the text file.
description: We broke the malware down into raw Assembly code. Read through the text file to figure out how the program jumps past the security check.

name: Unpacking UPX
description:
The malware was packed tightly to hide its code. We dumped it out of the computer's memory while it was running and found this string. Grab the flag:

0x08048000: tcs{upx_unpacked_manual}

name: Custom Virtual Machine
clue: Read the pushes backward from right to left.
description:
The malware runs in its own weird virtual machine! We caught the commands it sent to the memory stack. Read this sequence backwards to build the flag:

PUSH '}'; PUSH 'd'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 's'; PUSH 'r'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 'v'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 'r'; PUSH '_'; PUSH 'e'; PUSH 'd'; PUSH 'o'; PUSH 'c'; PUSH 'p'; PUSH 'o'; PUSH '{'; PUSH 's'; PUSH 'c'; PUSH 't';

name: Android Manifest
description: We decompiled a sketchy Android app. Look inside the AndroidManifest.xml file to see if they accidentally exported a hidden activity to the public.

name: Hardcoded Keys
clue: Extract the key from inside the XML tags.
description:
Rule #1 of app development: Never hardcode your API keys! We found this snippet in the app's strings.xml file. Grab the flag:

<string name="prod_api_key">tcs{strings_xml_key}</string>

name: Insecure Broadcast
description:
The Android app was shouting sensitive info to the whole phone! We intercepted this system broadcast. Grab the flag from the payload data:

action="com.tcs.admin.AUTH" payload="tcs{intent_intercepted}"
